procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 12.03.2021 of the High Court of Judicature at Patna in CRLM No.42776 of 2013.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Patna dismissed Criminal Miscellaneous No.42776 of 2013, which was a petition to quash First Information Report No.87 of 2011 dated 19.03.2011 registered at Dumraon Police Station, Buxar, Bihar under Sections 467, 468, 469 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. During the pendency of the case in High Court, the appellant filed Interlocutory Application No.1261 of 2017 seeking amendment of the prayer to include quashing of the order dated 18.11.2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order refusing to quash the FIR. The State of Bihar filed a counter-affidavit opposing the appeal and justifying the prosecution. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The parties are to bear their own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether a dispute between a Power of Attorney (PoA) holder and the principals regarding the payment of sale consideration is purely a civil matter, into which the vendee should not be dragged.

facts: A vendee (the appellant) purchased land and paid the entire sale consideration to the Power of Attorney (PoA) holder.
The landowners (principals) who granted the PoA alleged that their PoA holder did not pay them the money received from the sale.
The principals initiated criminal proceedings (FIR) against the vendee for fraud and other offenses.
The vendee had no role in the execution of the PoA between the principals and their agent, nor in any alleged misdeed by the PoA holder towards the principals.
law: The Court interpreted the Power of Attorney document by applying a principle of harmonious construction to its clauses (specifically Clauses 3, 11, and 15).
The Court found that Clauses 3 and 11 clearly authorized the PoA holder to execute sale deeds and receive the sale consideration on behalf of the principals.
Clause 15, which allowed the PoA holder to register deeds signed by the principals themselves, was interpreted as an additional power, not a limitation on the authority granted in the other clauses.
application: Based on the PoA's terms, the Court determined that the PoA holder was legally authorized to sell the property and receive the payment from the vendee.
Since the vendee paid the full consideration to the authorized agent (the PoA holder), the vendee fulfilled their legal obligation.
The core issue is the dispute between the principals and their own agent (the PoA holder) over the money. This is an internal financial dispute.

The Court reasoned that it would be improper to drag the vendee into this internal dispute, especially through criminal litigation, as the vendee had no part in the relationship or alleged wrongdoing between the principals and their agent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the dispute over whether the PoA holder paid the sale consideration to the principals is a civil matter between those two parties. The Court held that the vendee, having paid the full consideration to the authorized agent and having no role in their internal dispute, should not be dragged into the matter, particularly through criminal proceedings. Consequently, the FIR against the vendee was quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a vendee, who has paid the full consideration to a Power of Attorney (PoA) holder and had no role in the execution of the PoA or any alleged misdeed by the holder, can be subjected to criminal litigation.

facts: A vendee (the appellant) purchased property from a person holding a Power of Attorney (PoA) from the landowners.
The vendee paid the entire consideration amount for the property to the PoA holder.
The landowners filed a criminal FIR against the PoA holder and the vendee, alleging misappropriation, fraud, and misuse of the PoA.
The vendee had no part in the creation of the PoA document.
The vendee was not involved in any alleged misdeed by the PoA holder concerning the landowners, such as the failure to remit the sale proceeds.
A separate civil suit filed by the landowners against the vendee regarding the same property sale had already been dismissed in the vendee's favor.
law: A court can quash criminal proceedings to protect an individual from unwanted criminal prosecution and unnecessary trial, especially when the dispute is primarily civil in nature.
A person cannot be held criminally liable for the misdeeds of another if they had no role in or knowledge of those acts.
The specific terms of a Power of Attorney document determine the authority granted to the holder.
application: The Court examined the PoA and found that it explicitly authorized the holder to execute sale deeds and receive consideration on behalf of the landowners.
The Court determined that the vendee's only role was to purchase the property and pay the agreed-upon price to the authorized agent (the PoA holder), which the vendee did.
The Court reasoned that the actual dispute was a civil matter between the landowners (principals) and their agent (the PoA holder) over the money received from the sale.

Since the vendee had no role in the execution of the PoA or the subsequent dispute between the principals and their agent, the Court found it would be improper to drag the vendee into the criminal litigation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the vendee, having paid the full consideration to an authorized PoA holder and having no role in the PoA's execution or the agent's alleged misdeeds, should not be subjected to criminal litigation. The Court quashed the FIR and all related proceedings against the vendee.

issue.issue_text: Whether the courts at Dehradun have the territorial jurisdiction to examine a dispute concerning a Sale Deed executed in Dehradun for a property located in Dehradun.

facts: A Power of Attorney (PoA) was executed in Buxar.
Using this PoA, a Sale Deed was executed and registered in Dehradun.
The property subject to the Sale Deed is located in Dehradun.
The execution of the PoA itself is not in dispute.
The central controversy relates only to the execution of the Sale Deed.
law: Territorial jurisdiction is determined by where the cause of action arises.
application: The Supreme Court distinguished between the execution of the PoA and the execution of the Sale Deed.
It noted that while the PoA was executed in Buxar, this was merely one link in the chain of events and was not the subject of the dispute.
The actual dispute, or the 'cause of action', stemmed from the execution of the Sale Deed.
All events related to the Sale Deed—its execution, the registration, and the location of the property—occurred in Dehradun.
Therefore, the Court reasoned that the factual basis for the dispute clearly placed it within the jurisdiction of the Dehradun courts.
The Court explicitly stated that these facts did not give rise to any cause of action in Buxar.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the courts at Dehradun have the territorial jurisdiction to examine the dispute, as the entire cause of action related to the Sale Deed arose in Dehradun.

issue.issue_text: Whether the dismissal of a prior civil suit filed by the landowners for the same cause of action in favour of the vendee is a relevant factor in deciding to quash subsequent criminal proceedings.

facts: The landowners had previously filed a civil suit (Original Suit No. 27 of 2011) at Dehradun concerning the same property transaction that was the subject of the later criminal FIR.
This civil suit was for the same cause of action and was filed prior to the FIR.
The civil court dismissed the suit in favour of the vendee (the appellant in the criminal case).
In its judgment, the civil court specifically held that the Power of Attorney (PoA) holder had the right to sell the land and that the sale deed executed in favour of the vendee was valid.
law: The Court analyzed Sections 40 to 43 of the Evidence Act, which determine when a judgment from a prior case is relevant in a subsequent case.

The Court established that while a civil judgment is not automatically conclusive or a bar to a criminal proceeding on the same facts, it is a relevant factor whose effect must be decided based on the specifics of each case.

The Court cited a precedent (*Mukul Agrawal v State of Uttar Pradesh*) which held that a civil court's finding that a document was not forged could cause the "very substratum of the criminal complaint" to vanish, justifying the quashing of the criminal case.
application: The Supreme Court applied these legal principles to the facts, noting that the prior civil court judgment had already adjudicated the core issue at the heart of the criminal complaint.
The civil court's specific finding that the sale deed was valid directly contradicted the criminal allegations of fraud and misappropriation related to that same deed.

The Court reasoned that since the validity of the transaction had been upheld in a civil proceeding between the same parties, continuing a criminal prosecution against the vendee on the same grounds would be an abuse of the process of law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the dismissal of the prior civil suit in the vendee's favour was a highly relevant and decisive factor. Because the civil court had already validated the very transaction that formed the basis of the criminal allegations, the foundation of the criminal case was effectively removed. Therefore, the Court concluded that this prior civil judgment justified quashing the subsequent criminal proceedings against the vendee.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a dispute between a Power of Attorney (PoA) holder and the principals regarding the payment of sale consideration is purely a civil matter, into which the vendee should not be dragged.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (vendee) argued that the dispute is between the landowners and their PoA holder, and the appellant should not be involved.
It was contended that the PoA was valid, not forged or withdrawn, and it explicitly entitled the holder to execute deeds and receive consideration on behalf of the landowners.

Since the appellant paid valuable consideration to the authorized PoA holder, the appellant cannot be held liable for any subsequent misdeed by the holder, implying the issue is a civil dispute between the other parties.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the appellant should remain part of the criminal proceedings, submitting that the Trial Court should be allowed to exercise its power under Section 319, CrPC against the appellant if warranted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a vendee, who has paid the full consideration to a Power of Attorney (PoA) holder and had no role in the execution of the PoA or any alleged misdeed by the holder, can be subjected to criminal litigation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant is merely the vendee of the land covered by a valid PoA.
The appellant paid valuable consideration for the sale as required.
Given that the PoA was admittedly not forged and the appellant paid the consideration, the appellant cannot be held liable for any misdeed by the PoA holder, much less be subjected to a criminal act.
respondent_arguments: The respondent contended that the vendee (appellant) could still be implicated, suggesting that the Trial Court should be permitted to use its power under Section 319, CrPC to proceed against the appellant if evidence warranted it.

cases.principle: When clauses in a deed or contract cannot be reconciled, the earlier clause prevails over the later clause.

cases.case_name: Radha Sundar Dutta v Mohd. Jahadur Rahim
cases.principle: For approvingly taking note of the proposition that when clauses in a deed or contract cannot be reconciled, the earlier clause prevails over the later clause.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When interpreting a deed or contract, the court must first attempt a harmonious construction of all clauses to ensure that each is given effect and none are rendered ineffective.
obiter: If clauses in a deed or contract cannot be reconciled, the earlier clause will prevail over a later clause that is repugnant to it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the dispute was fundamentally a civil matter between the landowners (principals) and their Power of Attorney holder concerning the payment of sale consideration. The appellant, as the vendee who paid the full consideration to the authorized PoA holder, should not be subjected to criminal prosecution for this internal family and civil dispute. Allowing the criminal proceedings to continue against the vendee would constitute an abuse of the legal process.
legal_tests_applied: When interpreting a deed or contract, if an earlier clause conflicts with a later clause and they cannot be reconciled, the earlier clause will prevail over the later one.

Where a civil court has made a conclusive finding on a central fact, such as a document not being forged, the 'very substratum of the criminal complaint vanishes,' and allowing the criminal prosecution to continue would be a complete abuse of the process of law.
In an appropriate case, the court will exercise its power to quash criminal proceedings to accord protection against unwanted criminal prosecution and the prospect of an unnecessary trial.
policy_considerations: The judicial system must provide protection to individuals against unwanted criminal prosecution and the prospect of an unnecessary trial, especially when the dispute is clearly civil in nature.

A bona fide purchaser for value (vendee) who has fulfilled their obligations by paying the agreed consideration to a duly authorized agent (PoA holder) should not be dragged into subsequent civil or criminal controversies between the agent and their principals.
Permitting a criminal prosecution to proceed after a civil court has rendered a conclusive finding on the core issue would amount to a complete abuse of the process of law.
